Title: "Contributing"
This guide is for someone who wants to build the library, run its tests and gates, and open a pull request. It
covers the tools on Windows, Linux and macOS, the build step by step, the gates every change must pass, and how a
pull request is reviewed and released. The design document describes what is underneath.
Tools
  Tool   Needed for   Version  
    
  .NET SDK   Everything   10.0, as  pins it (, so any 10.0.x feature band serves)  
  PowerShell 7   The repository build script, the Unicode table generators, the site build   7.4 or later  
  Git   The repository and the test data   Any recent version  
  Node.js   The test data generator (in the data repository) and the documentation site's search index   24 for the data generator (the V8 it carries is the oracle); 20 or later for the site  
  Python 3   Writing the record of a benchmark run   3.10 or later  
  GitHub CLI   The documentation site only (it fetches the site generator)   Any recent version  
A contributor who only builds the library and runs its tests needs the .NET SDK and Git. PowerShell is needed for
the repository build script and the tools; the site and the benchmark tools need the rest.
Windows
Open a new terminal after the installs so that  is current. The repository builds in Windows Terminal,
PowerShell 7 or Developer PowerShell; Visual Studio 2022 17.14 or later and Visual Studio Code with the C# Dev Kit
both open .
Linux
The .NET SDK is best installed with Microsoft's install script, which puts it under your home directory and never
conflicts with a distribution package:
On Ubuntu and Debian the SDK is also in Microsoft's package feed () as ;
on Fedora, . Whichever route you take,  must show a 10.0 SDK.
PowerShell 7 comes as a package ( from Microsoft's feed on Ubuntu and Debian, 
on Fedora,  elsewhere) or as a .NET tool: . Node.js 24 is in the NodeSource feed or as a binary tarball from nodejs.org; Python 3, Git and the
GitHub CLI () are in every distribution's repositories.
The benchmark procedure pins the run to a set of cores with , which is part of  and already
installed.
macOS
Add  to  if Homebrew does not link the versioned Node. On Apple silicon the
SDK is native arm64; the vectorised paths run on NEON through , and the searches that have an AVX2 form
(the packed needle and the fingerprint search, section 4.3 of the design) take their  form, so every
test passes, but benchmark numbers are not comparable with the published run, which is on x64.
Getting the sources
The test data repository is the oracle for the engine (design, section 8). It is not vendored, so clone it beside
the library; the commands below assume .
Building and testing, step by step
Every command runs from the repository root. The solution file is .

title: Corvus.Regex.Ecma262: design
description: What the library is and where it came from, the public surface, one matcher over two encodings, the searches for a start, the source generator, the target frameworks, the test data and the benchmarks.
body:
ContentType: "application/vnd.endjin.ssg.content+md"
PublicationStatus: Published
Date: 2026-10-20T00:00:00.0+00:00
Title: "Corvus.Regex.Ecma262: design"
This document describes the library as it is: what it offers, how the engine is built, why the decisions that
shape it were taken, and how it is tested and measured. The getting-started pages on the
documentation site show how to use it; this document is for a
reader who wants to know what is underneath, or who intends to change it.
What it is
A regular expression library for .NET whose grammar and answers are those of ECMA-262 (ECMAScript 2025), with the
public shape of , so that a project moves to it by changing a  directive and
its options. It includes a build-time source generator with the shape of . It matches UTF-8
text natively, in addition to UTF-16, and a match allocates nothing once the per-thread working memory has grown.
It is its own library in its own repository, , and its own NuGet package,
so that it can be used anywhere. Corvus.JsonSchema, whose  and  keywords are defined
over ECMA-262 expressions, is its first intended consumer; the adoption is a separate decision, taken on the
benchmarks of section 9.
Why ECMA-262 and not .NET's grammar. JSON Schema, OpenAPI and many wire formats specify their patterns as
ECMAScript regular expressions. .NET's engine reads a different grammar with different classes ( and 
are Unicode in .NET, ASCII in ECMA-262), a different case-folding rule and a different notion of a line
terminator. A translation layer from one to the other can never be exact, and the shapes it cannot translate
have to be refused or interpreted by hand. An engine that reads the ECMA-262 grammar directly, held to the same
answers as V8 over a large data set (section 8), removes the translation and its exceptions.
Origins: what is ported and from where
The Corvus JSON Schema ports in Go, Rust, Object Pascal and OCaml each carry an ECMA-262 engine, one design in
four copies, and the C# code generator carries a parser of its own. The library was built from those rather than
from nothing:
  Piece   Source   Notes  
    
  Parser, syntax tree, both grammars (the u flag; Annex B without), group names, modifier groups    from Corvus.JsonSchema's code generator   Already C#, already netstandard2.0, already Unicode 17 and ECMAScript 2025. The base of the front end.  
  Unicode property tables, case folding (Canonicalize for both modes), sets   ,  (generated) and the Go  package   The generator script  moved with them.  
  Compiler (tree to flat program), instruction set   The Go and Rust  compilers   Characters, sets, literals, anchors, splits, captures, lookarounds, counted loops, backreferences in four forms.  
  Backtracking matcher: explicit stack, memo of failed places, counted loops, first sets, time and memory limits   The Go and Rust virtual machines   The Rust form (per-thread state, retained capacity) is the closer model for .NET.  
  ASCII automaton for linear patterns   The Go and Rust automata   256 states, built on first use.  
  Anchored, forward and reverse automata, and the window of positions read one unit at a time    of the Rust engine (corvus-regex-ecma262-rs), from the  crate's automata and V8's Boyer-Moore lookahead   Up to 2,048 states, built on the first search that wants them (section 4.4).  
  Matching by UTF-16 code unit over UTF-8 text   The Go and Rust  cursors   The position between the halves of a four-byte character is the offset of its third byte.  
  Resource limits   The Rust parser's limits and cost model   Pattern nesting, program size, construction cost, match time, backtracking memory.  
Each file records its provenance. The v flag (section 3.2) and everything in sections 4.3, 4.4 and 5 beyond the
instruction interpreter were written for this library and have since been carried back to the ports where they
apply.
Public surface
3.1 Names and namespace
The types are named as .NET names them: , , , , ,
, , , , ,
, . The options type is not : it is ,
the flags of ECMA-262 (section 3.2). Moving a project to the library is a change of  plus a change of its
options; that break in source compatibility was accepted so that the options say what the engine does rather than
carry .NET options the engine cannot honour.
The namespace is , which mirrors , and the
package id is . The namespace cannot contain a segment named : C# resolves a simple
name by walking the enclosing namespaces before it reads the  directives of the compilation unit, so inside
 the name  would bind to a namespace  and not to the type, and
any consumer in a  namespace would hit the same.
3.2 Flags
The options are ECMA-262's flags and nothing else: a  with one member for each flag of
, and a constructor that also takes the flags as the string  takes.
  Member   Flag   Meaning

title: Benchmarks: the Industry workloads
description: What the Industry benchmarks measure, where the daily run publishes the figures, and where this library is slower than .NET and why.
body:
ContentType: "application/vnd.endjin.ssg.content+md"
PublicationStatus: Published
Date: 2026-10-20T00:00:00.0+00:00
Title: "Benchmarks: the Industry workloads"
Corvus.Regex.Ecma262 is faster than  across the board. On the Industry
workloads that .NET itself publishes figures for, its interpreter beats .NET's interpreter on all but one or two of
the 57, taking about half the time at the median and under a fifth at the geometric mean; its generated code is at
or below .NET's generated code on about four workloads in five over UTF-16 and nine in ten over UTF-8, where it takes
about half the time at the median; and both are far ahead of V8, which takes six times longer at the median. The
exact figures are on the benchmark page, every engine measured on one runner each night.
The library is measured against  and against V8 on the Industry workload set of
dotnet/performance (): the Sherlock Holmes text and
the Rust  patterns, the Leipzig corpus searches, the mariomka email, URI and IPv4 patterns, and the rebar
name searches over Russian and Chinese subtitles. These are the sets behind .NET's own "regex performance
improvements in .NET N" posts, so the figures can be read beside theirs.
The figures
The figures are on one page, corvus-oss.org/corvus-regex-ecma262-benchmarks. Each night it runs every Corvus
ECMA-262 engine's published harness image, this library's among them, one after another on one runner, so every
figure on it was measured on the same machine in the same hour. Pick the engines and the measure, and read the
leaderboard, the matrix of every workload, one workload at a time with its spread, or two engines head to head.
Each engine's ECMA-262 compliance is beside its name, its header says which release of each engine ran, and every
day's data is kept.
No figure is repeated here: a table in a document goes stale the night after it is written, and the page does not.
What is measured
Six engines, each counting the matches of every workload over its whole text (, one call per operation):
  Engine   What it is  
   
  .NET interpreter    with   
  .NET generated    through   
  Corvus interpreter   this library's interpreter over UTF-16  
  Corvus generated UTF-16   this library's source generator over UTF-16  
  Corvus generated UTF-8   this library's source generator over the same text as UTF-8 bytes, nothing transcoded  
  V8 (Node 24)   Node's , the oracle of the test data, over the same texts, counted by a  loop that advances  as  does ()  
The Corvus and V8 rows run under the  flag, which .NET has no mode for, so the two read a few rows by different
rules: counts agree with .NET on 53 of the 57 workloads, and the four apart are  and  at CRLF, where ECMA-262
counts CR as a line terminator, and , which .NET takes as Unicode letters and digits.
The figures on the benchmark page are measured under the interleaved protocol of every Corvus engine's harness
(, ): every workload in turn, each in three rounds
of the engines in turn, their order turned each round, each figure a process of its own, warmed for at least 1.5 s
(.NET compiles a method again as it is used, and needs that long to reach its final code) and timed for 0.7 s in seven
passes. The bar is the median of the rounds and the whisker the fastest and the slowest round; a row's ratio is read
against its neighbours' rather than to the last few percent. The BenchmarkDotNet classes of the same project
(, ) measure the same counts under the pinned-host procedure, with what each
allocates; the library allocates nothing per match once its working memory has grown.
Where this library is slower than .NET, and why
Four kinds of row read above 1.0 against .NET's generated code, each the price of an ECMA-262 rule that .NET does
not apply:
and  at CRLF. ECMA-262's  stops at CR as well as LF, so over a text with CRLF endings  finds
   36,491 matches to .NET's 26,105, at parity per match.
Case-insensitive patterns under the u flag. The search must find the long s and the Kelvin sign as forms of
    and , which .NET's search ignores, so its tables carry every form ( with ).
A class that admits a supplementary character before a literal at a fixed distance. Such a character is two
   units, so the distance is not fixed and the literal is found by a walk back rather than at an offset
   ().
Non-ASCII literals over UTF-8. Every Cyrillic or Chinese character is two or three bytes with no rare byte
   among them, where UTF-16 gives the search one rare unit per character; so the UTF-8 rows for the Chinese names
   read above .NET over UTF-16 while the UTF-16 rows are level.
The other rows above 1.0 are within a few percent of parity and read either side of it from run to run: both engines
are at the floor of one vectorised search over the text.
V8 has no vectorised search for a literal, a set or an alternation beyond its first character, so the rows that such
a search decides read tens to hundreds of times slower there; the rows it wins are short fixed literals over

title: Getting Started
description: Install Corvus.Regex.Ecma262, write a pattern with the flags of ECMA-262, match over strings and over UTF-8 without allocating, and generate the matcher at build time with [GeneratedRegex].
keywords: getting started installation regex ECMA-262 source generator C# tutorial UTF-8
body:
Introduction
Corvus.Regex.Ecma262 is a regular expression engine that answers as ECMAScript does. Where  has its own grammar and its own meaning for , , , , case folding and Unicode properties, this engine has ECMA-262's, so a pattern written for JavaScript, or taken from a JSON Schema, matches the same texts here as it does there.
This guide covers:
Setup — the one package, and what it brings.
Patterns and flags — the flags are ECMA-262's letters, not , and what each one does.
Matching — the members you know from , and the allocation-free forms beside them.
UTF-8 — the same patterns over  with no transcoding.
The source generator —  and what it generates.
Differences from .NET's Regex — what to expect when the two meet.
Setup
One package carries the library and the source generator:
The library targets  and . The vectorised searches and the generated search code need the .NET 10 or later runtime. The  build is for .NET Framework, where the same patterns give the same answers by the plain paths. .NET 8 and .NET 9 are not supported.
Patterns and flags
A pattern is written as it would be in JavaScript, and the flags are the letters  takes, as a string or as the  enumeration:
  Flag      Meaning  
    
        Accepted for completeness; indices are always kept.  
         replaces every match; without it, the first, as  does.  
        Canonicalize of the mode in force: simple case folding with  or ,  without. Never the culture.  
         and  at line terminators.  
        The dot matches line terminators.  
        The  flag grammar; matched by code point.  
        Set notation and properties of strings; matched by code point.  and  together is a syntax error, as in ECMA-262.  
        A match only at the start position.  
With no flag the pattern is read with the Annex B grammar and matched by UTF-16 code unit, which is what ECMA-262 does with no flag. JSON Schema's reading, the  flag first and Annex B when that refuses, is two calls of , which costs no exception:
A pattern that is not valid throws , with the reason and the offset. Every pattern has deterministic limits of size, and  says when one is passed.
Matching
The members are the ones of , with the same names and the same shapes:
, , ,  with a string and  with a string allocate what they return, as .NET's do: that is the drop-in shape. The span members beside them allocate nothing:
,  and  are the global search whether or not  is set. Where ECMA-262 keeps  on the , the library takes the position as an argument:  is  with  set, and  anchors it there. A  has no mutable state, so one instance is safe to share between threads.
A match that reaches its limit of time () or of memory throws , whatever the pattern. An instance made without a timeout takes : the  data of the , which  reads too, and no timeout when it is not set. Without a timeout a match has no limit of time or of memory, so a program that matches patterns or texts from outside should set one, for example with  when it starts.
UTF-8
Every member that takes a  has a twin that takes UTF-8 bytes, and the engine matches the bytes as they are. Nothing is transcoded, and the positions it gives are byte offsets.
Under the  and  flags a character is a code point in both encodings, so a class, a dot or a quantifier takes a four-byte sequence as one character. With no flag ECMA-262 matches by UTF-16 code unit; over UTF-8 the engine keeps that meaning, so a pattern with no flag gives the same answers over the bytes of a text as over its chars, except where the text holds a lone surrogate, which UTF-8 cannot hold.
The source generator
 on a partial method or a partial property writes the matcher as code at build time, in the shape of .NET's own attribute (a partial property needs C# 13, which  has by default; on  set  to 13 or use a method). The pattern and the flags are checked by the generator: a pattern that is not valid, a flag that is not one, or  with , is a build error with the reason and the position.
The member returns one  each time, built on the generated code. The generated code is the search for where a match can start and the match itself as structured code, over both encodings. A pattern too large for straight-line code (a class of thousands of strings, such as ) is handed to the interpreter by its generated runner, so every pattern compiles.
The generator ships in the same package and runs on the  build of the library, as a source generator must.
Differences from .NET's Regex
The surface follows ; the meaning follows ECMA-262. The differences a user coming from .NET will meet:
The grammar. No  inline option (ECMA-262 has  groups), no atomic groups, no possessive quantifiers, no  and , no conditionals, no balancing groups.  is the letter  under Annex B and an error under .
The character classes.  is ,  is the 63 ASCII word characters,  is ECMAScript's white space and line terminators, and  excludes the four line terminators (LF, CR, U+2028, U+2029).
Case. With  and , simple case folding

body:
A drop-in replacement for System.Text.RegularExpressions that answers as ECMAScript does, with performance equal to or better than .NET's on equivalent expressions: over UTF-8 and over UTF-16, with no allocation per match and a build-time source generator.
The answers of ECMAScript
The grammar and the semantics of ECMAScript 2025: lookbehind, named groups, modifier groups, Unicode property escapes on Unicode 17 data, and the  and  flags with set notation and strings in classes. Tested against V8's answers for every pattern of the ECMA-262 regular expression test data, test262's patterns and exec calls among them, with none wrong.
Two encodings, one matcher
Matching over UTF-8 () and over UTF-16 (, ) with no transcoding either way, from the same engine.
Zero allocation per match
Nothing is allocated once the per-thread working memory has grown. , , ,  into an  and  give the allocation-free forms of every member.
The shape of System.Text.RegularExpressions
, , , , , ,  and , in the namespace , so the library drops in where the .NET class is used.
A source generator
 on a partial method or property writes the matcher as code at build time, with the pattern checked and reported as a build error.
Bounded in time and memory
A backtracking matcher that remembers where a way has failed, a deterministic automaton for the patterns that need no backtracking, a limit of time and of memory on every match, and deterministic limits of size on every pattern.
